SERIES: Could You Survive ,  One deadly situation per episode. You wake up inside it — every decision is yours, and most people choose wrong.

ART STYLE (auto-prefixed to every shot at production):
Visceral first-person survival cinema — a photoreal, grounded 9:16 vertical thriller that puts the viewer INSIDE one life-or-death situation per episode. Every shot looks like a real place with real physics: authentic terrain, weather, water, fire, snow, machinery and equipment, rich atmospheric detail (spindrift, smoke, silt, embers, heat shimmer) and natural, motivated light only. Shallow depth of field, subtle handheld urgency on close shots, vast awe-inducing wides for scale; immersive eye-level and over-the-shoulder framing that makes the danger personal. A single recurring man — 'the survivor', the channel's face — is the viewer's body inside the scene: he NEVER speaks, lip-syncs or mouths words (his voice is added afterward as narration). His clothing always matches the scenario and is stated explicitly per shot. Intense, physical and frightening in scale but NEVER gory, bloody or graphic — the danger lives in physics, time and distance, not in injury detail. No captions, no subtitles, no on-screen text, no logos or watermarks.

CREATIVE BRIEF for new episodes:
Sonsuz ikinci-şahıs HAYATTA KALMA antolojisi. Her bölüm izleyiciyi ('you') — ekranda kanalın yüzü 'ihsan_survivor' ile temsil edilir — GERÇEK, yüksek-ilgi bir ölüm-kalım durumunun içine bırakır ve KARAR KARAR yaşatır. Milyonların zaten arattığı, öğretici değeri kanıtlanmış senaryolar seç ('could you survive an avalanche', 'how to escape a sinking car' gibi aramaların karşılığı). (2) Anlatım = İKİNCİ şahıs ('you'), ŞİMDİKİ zaman, MrBallen gerilimi ama öğretici PAYOFF'lu: tehlikeyi ve süreyi/sayıyı adlayan tok bir KANCA cümlesiyle AÇ; ortada izleyiciye 1-2 gerçek KARAR sorusu sor ('do you dig immediately?' gibi) ve yanlış seçimin NEDEN öldürdüğünü söyle; DOĞRU hamleyi ve nedenini ver — payoff GERÇEK, kanıtlanabilir hayatta-kalma bilgisidir (uydurma istatistik YASAK: kesin sayıyı yalnız eminsen kullan, değilsen 'most people' de); SON cümle HER ZAMAN izleyiciye yorum sorusudur ('What would you have done? Tell me below.' — bölümden bölüme çeşitlendir). 82-96 kelime; son cümle ~44. saniyeye kadar bitmeli. (3) 'ihsan_survivor' en az 3-4 çekimde görünür; kıyafeti SENARYOYA UYGUN (kayak montu, sürücü kıyafeti, yürüyüş kıyafeti, dönem üniforması, çöl giysisi...) ve İhsan'ın göründüğü HER çekimin prompt'unda AÇIKÇA yeniden yazılır (character_id yalnız YÜZÜ kilitler, kıyafeti DEĞİL; boş bırakılan çekim yanlış gardıroba kayar); tarihsel bölümde dönem-doğru, modern bölümde senaryo-doğru giyinir; ASLA konuşmaz/dudak senkronu yapmaz. drowned-history.contents:
SERIES: Drowned History ,  Every artifact in this story is real — this is a dramatized reenactment of one of history's most haunting underwater discoveries.

ART STYLE (auto-prefixed to every shot at production):
Found-footage from a technical diver's helmet-mounted camera — a FICTIONAL dramatized reenactment of a real archaeological recovery operation. Vertical 9:16, first-person POV: the frame drifts and sways gently with the diver's slow fin kicks, occasionally a gloved hand, gauge or exhaled bubbles cross the frame. Deep dark water lit only by dive torches and headlamp beams — volumetric light cones full of drifting silt and marine snow, murky green-blue gloom fading to pure black at the edges, mild wide-lens distortion, soft focus shifts, light sensor grain. One or two teammate divers appear ahead as dark silhouettes with glowing torches; their faces are always hidden behind dive masks and regulators, never clearly visible. Atmospheric, ominous, awe-and-dread mood — haunting but never graphic or gory. No on-screen text, no captions, no logos, no watermarks (all overlays are added in post). IMPORTANT: this is a silent visual shot — do NOT render any person speaking, lip-sync or talking to camera; the voice is added separately as narration.

CREATIVE BRIEF for new episodes:
Each episode dramatizes ONE REAL underwater archaeological discovery as found-footage from a dive team's helmet camera. FIXED 5-SHOT ARC: (1) descent into dark water toward the site; (2) approach and entry — the site emerges from the murk and the team slips inside; (3) one eerie beat (statues staring, a sudden animal, impossible stillness); (4) THE FIND — torchlight lands on the artifact/subject (hook_shot=4); (5) recovery/documentation and ascent — gloved hands, lift bags or sample cases (if the site is protected, the team documents and takes NOTHING), then surface glow above, site fading below, one last haunting look. NARRATION: calm documentary-horror gravitas, past tense, built ONLY from the facts of the chosen FACT BANK entry — NEVER invent names, dates, objects or numbers. OPEN with a gripping first line of 10 words or fewer — a shocking number, a death, a stopped clock, or an impossible image — never a slow scene-setting throat-clear; land the single most astonishing fact inside the first two sentences; end with a line that lingers (what remains below, what we still cannot explain). Do not write the '~' character or any symbol the voice cannot read aloud — spell it 'about'. TITLE_CARD: title = the artifact/site name (max 40 chars); subtitle = 'Region, Country — found YEAR' (use 'flooded YEAR' / 'raised YEAR' / 'first mapped YEAR' / 'excavated YEAR-YEAR' when that fits the entry better). The YEAR is MANDATORY and must be a real 4-digit year copied DIRECTLY from the chosen FACT BANK entry — never omit, round, guess or invent a date; if the entry gives only a range, use that range. The title and subtitle are burned on-screen as the video's cover, so they must be spelled and dated exactly right. NEVER show human remains, skeletons or bodies on screen. FACT BANK — each episode uses EXACTLY ONE entry that no existing episode has used yet (check existing titles/synopses; always put the entry's name inside the synopsis): [1] Mary Rose — Solent, England — located 1971, raised 1982; Henry VIII's flagship, sank 1545; thousands of artifacts including hundreds of longbows. [2] Vasa — Stockholm harbor, Sweden — found 1956 by Anders Franzén, raised 1961 nearly intact; the great warship sank on her maiden voyage in 1628. [3] Riace Bronzes — off Riace, Calabria, Italy — found 1972 by a snorkeler at ~8 m; two full-size ancient Greek bronze warriors, c. 460-450 BC. [4] Kyrenia Ship — off Kyrenia, Cyprus — found 1965 by sponge diver Andreas Cariolou; 4th-century-BC Greek merchant ship, hull raised and displayed in Kyrenia Castle. [5] Cape Gelidonya wreck — off Antalya, Türkiye — excavated 1960 by George Bass; Late Bronze Age (~1200 BC) copper-ingot cargo; the first scientific underwater excavation in history. [6] Serçe Limanı Glass Wreck — near Marmaris, Türkiye — found 1973; 11th-century ship carrying three tons of Islamic glass; now in Bodrum. [7] Sunken Port Royal — Jamaica — two-thirds of the pirate city sank in the 1692 earthquake; excavations 1981-1990 recovered a pocket watch stopped near 11:43. [8] Cleopatra's royal quarter on Antirhodos — Alexandria harbor, Egypt — mapped from 1996 by Franck Goddio; sphinxes and priest statues found on the drowned island. [9] Pavlopetri — off Laconia, Greece — mapped 1968 by Nicholas Flemming; the world's oldest submerged town, Bronze Age streets and tombs at ~4 m. [10] Atlit-Yam — off Atlit, Israel — found 1984; a 9,000-year-old Neolithic village 8-12 m down, with a stone circle around a spring and the oldest known wells. [11] Belitung wreck — Java Sea, Indonesia — found 1998 by sea-cucumber divers; 9th-century Arabian dhow carrying ~60,000 Tang-dynasty ceramics and gold. [12] San José galleon — off Cartagena, Colombia — located 2015 by a deep-water robot at ~600 m; Spanish treasure galleon sunk in battle in 1708; its gold is still on the seabed. [13] Dokos wreck — off Dokos island, Greece — found 1975 by Peter Throckmorton; the oldest known shipwreck cargo on Earth, c. 2200 BC. [14] Nemi ships — Lake Nemi, Italy — Caligula's two giant pleasure barges recovered 1929-1932 by partly draining the sacred lake; both burned in 1944, bronze fittings survive. [15] Lake Titicaca offerings — Khoa Reef near the Island of the Sun, Bolivia — excavations 2013-2019 raised Inca and Tiwanaku stone offering boxes holding gold figurines and spondylus shell. [16] Grand Congloué — near Marseille, France — worked from 1952 by Jacques Cousteau's team; Roman-era wine-ship cargo of thousands of amphorae. [17] Yonaguni Monument — off Yonaguni, Japan — found 1986 by diver Kihachiro Aratake; colossal stepped stone terraces ~25 m down; scientists still dispute whether nature or human hands cut them (present honestly as an open mystery). [18] Bajo de la Campana — off Murcia, Spain — excavated 2007-2011; 7th-century-BC Phoenician ship carrying elephant tusks and raw ivory. [19] Mahdia wreck — off Mahdia, Tunisia — found 1907 by Greek sponge divers; Roman ship packed with Greek bronzes and sixty marble columns. [20] Mazotos wreck — off Mazotos, Cyprus — found 2006; 4th-century-BC merchantman with hundreds of wine amphorae still stacked as loaded. [21] Sinop D — Black Sea, off Sinop, Türkiye — found 2000 by Robert Ballard's team at ~320 m; a ~1,600-year-old ship so preserved in the oxygen-free dark that its mast still stands. [22] Rungholt — Wadden Sea, Germany — the trading town drowned in the great storm flood of 1362; in 2023 researchers located its lost church under the mudflats; legend says its bells still ring in storms. IF every FACT BANK entry has been used, choose another world-famous, thoroughly documented underwater discovery you are absolutely CERTAIN about (real name, real place, real year) and follow the same rules.
